implementation_notes: Rust keeps absence visible: Option<T> forces the caller to handle the missing case, so the pattern's 'just call it' promise applies to roles that own a benign behaviour rather than to missing data. The idiom there is a zero-sized value type with a Default implementation whose trait methods do nothing - exactly what the standard library does with io::sink() (a writer that consumes everything) and io::empty() (a reader that is always at EOF). Use an explicit special-case type when a collaborator may be absent and callers should not branch; use Option/Result when they must decide, because the type system will not let the decision be ignored.
pitfalls: A shared &'static special case requires the trait to be object-safe and the type to be Sync; borrowed or associated-type-heavy interfaces often force a Box per construction instead.

A no-op implementation that discards errors hides failures - the standard library's own convention is to return Result, so keep the special case for values whose failures are not the caller's business.
Do not fabricate an 'empty' instance with unsafe or mem::zeroed for a type without a valid all-zero state; implement Default explicitly and keep the invariant sound.
Default is a Rust-wide contract: implementing it as a benign no-op for a type that callers expect to be usable can hide a missing constructor call.
